correctness.rationale: For F(t)=t²−t+1, any solution with equal coordinates or a coordinate equal to 1 is (1,1). For 2≤a<b, put r=F(a)/b, a positive integer strictly less than a. The identity rb≡1 (mod a) and F(b)≡0 (mod a) imply b(1−b)≡1 (mod a), so r≡1−b (mod a), and F(1−b)=F(b). Therefore (r,a) obeys both divisibilities and has smaller sum. It cannot have r=1 when a>1. This confirms the unrestricted descent, including the boundary case. Grouping the defining sum by gcd gives nH(n)=∑_{d|n}dφ(d), a multiplicative numerator whose prime-power factor is (p^(2e+1)+1)/(p+1) and is 1 modulo p. This excludes every prime power in particular p and p². For distinct p,q the numerator is F(p)F(q), so integrality would force exactly the forbidden two-cycle. Together with H(1)=1 this establishes the stated squarefree consequence and prime graph assertions.
residual_risks: The proof does not exclude mixed higher powers at two primes or all longer prime cycles. The stored checker only samples finite ranges and is not the universal proof.

originality.rationale: Mills's 1953 Theorem 3 treats the exact negative-linear-sign system, within a stronger chain classification. Even without trusting the corrupted equality in extracted text, §2 and the §8 chain list imply this case: change both input signs, then any two adjacent negative terms in a 1-chain must both be −1. The reciprocal-gcd factorization is known, and the semiprime implication is just its application to that classified pair. A separate same-day indexed record explicitly states both results with the same hypotheses; its date does not determine ordering.
residual_risks: The theorem's last equality in the Mills extraction was not visually authenticated; the readable chain classification independently implies the exact result. No date ordering is asserted for the two indexed records. The review is not an exhaustive literature survey.
